tracks.narration: An AC voltage swings sinusoidally — but there's a clearer way to picture it: a rotating arrow.
Set up the complex plane. The voltage is an arrow of length V m, sitting at angle phi to the real axis.
Now spin it. As the arrow rotates at omega, its projection on the real axis traces the cosine wave you see on the right.
Add a second phasor lagging by ninety degrees. Both rotate together — and their two waves stay locked in phase difference.
Each AC voltage becomes one number — magnitude and angle — that you can add like a vector. No more integrating sines.
